fields.action: Reactivates acetylcholinesterase that has been inactivated by organophosphate pesticides or nerve agents. It binds to the organophosphate-enzyme complex, releases the phosphorus atom, and restores normal enzyme activity.
fields.forms: Injection: 600 mg/mL auto-injector, or vials containing 1 gram of powder for reconstitution.
fields.indication: Antidote for poisoning by organophosphate pesticides and nerve agents (used alongside atropine).
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to pralidoxime; poisoning by carbaryl or non-organophosphate substances (ineffective or can worsen toxicity).
fields.adverse: Rapid intravenous administration can cause laryngospasm, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and transient neuromuscular blockade.
fields.effects: Blurred vision, dizziness, headache, nausea, and mild local pain at the injection site.
fields.notes: Must be administered as early as possible after exposure, because "aging" of the phosphorylated enzyme makes it resistant to regeneration over time.

fields.action: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end-plate, preventing acetylcholine from binding and causing skeletal muscle relaxation.
fields.forms: Intravenous solution: 10 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate rapid sequence intubation (RSI) and routine endotracheal intubation, and to provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to rocuronium or bromide-containing compounds.
fields.adverse: Anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reactions, prolonged apnea, and severe bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Transient injection-site pain and mild, temporary changes in heart rate or blood pressure.
fields.notes: Features a relatively rapid onset of action compared to other non-depolarizing agents, making it an alternative to succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation when depolarizing blockers are contraindicated. Its effects can be rapidly reversed using sugammadex.

fields.action: Non-depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant that competes with acetylcholine for nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
fields.forms: Intravenous solution: 10 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Adjunct to general anesthesia to relax skeletal muscles and facilitate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation during surgical procedures.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to atracurium or besylate components.
fields.adverse: Histamine release leading to severe hypotension, flushing, bronchospasm, and cardiovascular collapse.
fields.effects: Skin flushing, erythema, transient hypotension, and mild wheezing.
fields.notes: Undergoes unique spontaneous degradation in plasma via Hofmann elimination (independent of liver or kidney function), making it useful in patients with hepatic or renal failure.

fields.action: Short-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competitively blocks nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
fields.forms: Intravenous solution: 2 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Adjunct to general anesthesia for short surgical procedures to relax skeletal muscles and facilitate tracheal intubation.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to mivacurium and patients with homozygous atypical plasma cholinesterase activity.
fields.adverse: Profound histamine release causing profound transient hypotension, flushing, and bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Cutaneous flushing, transient decrease in blood pressure, and mild tachycardia.
fields.notes: Metabolized primarily by plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase); patients with genetic deficiencies in this enzyme experience significantly prolonged paralysis.

fields.action: Long-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competes with acetylcholine at the motor end-plate.
fields.forms: Intravenous injection: 1 mg/mL, 2 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Facilitation of endotracheal intubation and provision of skeletal muscle relaxation during long surgical procedures or mechanical ventilation.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to pancuronium or bromides; situations where tachycardia is hazardous.
fields.adverse: Prolonged neuromuscular blockade, residual paralysis, and hypersensitivity reactions.
fields.effects: Tachycardia (due to vagolytic action and blockade of cardiac muscarinic receptors), hypertension, and increased salivation.
fields.notes: Unlike many other muscle relaxants, it typically increases heart rate and blood pressure instead of dropping it, due to its mild blocking action on cardiac vagal receptors.

fields.action: Prototype non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively inhibits acetylcholine at the skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors.
fields.forms: Intravenous injection: 3 mg/mL (Historical/classic pharmacological agent).
fields.indication: Historical agent used as an adjunct to general anesthesia for muscle relaxation and intubation.
fields.contraindication: Myasthenia gravis, severe electrolyte disturbances, and hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Significant histamine release causing marked hypotension, shock-like symptoms, and bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Hypotension, cutaneous flushing, respiratory depression, and reflex tachycardia.
fields.notes: Rarely used in modern clinical practice due to its high propensity for causing histamine-induced hypotension; largely superseded by safer non-depolarizing agents like rocuronium or atracurium.

fields.action: Acts centrally on the cough center in the medulla to elevate the threshold for coughing. (Note: Structurally related to opioids, it acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin reuptake inhibitor at high doses, sitting outside traditional cholinergic pathways).
fields.forms: Oral syrup: 5 mg/5 mL, 10 mg/5 mL, 15 mg/5 mL. Lozenges/tablets: 10 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg. Extended-release suspension: 30 mg/5 mL.
fields.indication: Temporary relief of coughs caused by minor throat and bronchial irritation (such as that accompanying a common cold).
fields.contraindication: Concurrent use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of stopping them (risk of severe serotonin syndrome).
fields.adverse: Serotonin syndrome (when combined with serotonergic drugs), acute psychosis, and respiratory depression at massive toxic/recreational doses.
fields.effects: Drowsiness, dizziness, mild gastrointestinal upset, and nervousness.
fields.notes: Widely used over-the-counter antitussive, but listed here as part of your source sheet context; abuse potential exists at very high supra-therapeutic doses due to its NMDA antagonist properties.

fields.action: Intermediate-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that competitively binds to nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, blocking the actions of acetylcholine.
fields.forms: Powder for intravenous injection: 10 mg/vial, 20 mg/vial.
fields.indication: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation and provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to vecuronium or bromide-containing compounds.
fields.adverse: Prolonged paralysis, anaphylaxis, and acute myopathy with prolonged use in intensive care settings.
fields.effects: Minimal hemodynamic changes, slight transient changes in heart rate.
fields.notes: Lacks significant cardiovascular side effects (does not cause notable histamine release or tachycardia), making it versatile for patients with cardiac disease. Can be reversed rapidly with sugammadex.

fields.action: Non-selective alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. It stimulates the heart, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, and causes systemic vasoconstriction.
fields.forms: Injection: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) and 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000). Auto-injector (EpiPen): 0.3 mg, 0.15 mg. Inhalation solution: 1%.
fields.indication: Emergency treatment of severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis), cardiac arrest, acute asthma attacks, and induction of local anesthesia prolongation.
fields.contraindication: Close-angle glaucoma, shock other than anaphylactic shock, known hypersensitivity, and during labor (when vasopressor effects may delay delivery).
fields.adverse: Hypertensive crisis, ventricular arrhythmias, cerebral hemorrhage, and pulmonary edema.
fields.effects: Tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, headache, and pale appearance.
fields.notes: It is the primary drug of choice for acute anaphylaxis; sensitive to light and air, meaning discolored solutions should be discarded.

fields.action: Potent alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist, with lesser beta-1 agonist activity. It causes intense peripheral vasoconstriction and moderate inotropic stimulation of the heart.
fields.forms: Intravenous infusion concentrate: 1 mg/mL (as base).
fields.indication: Treatment of severe acute hypotension and shock states (e.g., septic shock, cardiogenic shock) after fluid resuscitation.
fields.contraindication: Mesenteric or peripheral vascular thrombosis (unless absolutely necessary), profound hypovolemia, and known hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Severe tissue necrosis upon extravasation, reflex bradycardia, severe hypertension, and decreased organ perfusion.
fields.effects: Anxiety, transient headache, respiratory difficulty, and bradycardia.
fields.notes: Must be administered via a central venous catheter when possible to avoid severe extravasation injury; if extravasation occurs, phentolamine is used locally to counteract necrosis.

fields.action: Acts on dopaminergic receptors (D_1 and D_2) as well as beta-1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in a dose-dependent manner (renal/mesenteric vasodilation at low doses, cardiac stimulation at medium doses, and systemic vasoconstriction at high doses).
fields.forms: Intravenous infusion: 40 mg/mL, 80 mg/mL, 160 mg/mL. Premixed bags: 0.8 mg/mL to 3.2 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Correction of hemodynamic imbalances in shock syndromes due to myocardial infarction, trauma, septic endotoxemia, and congestive heart failure.
fields.contraindication: Pheochromocytoma, uncorrected tachyarrhythmias, and ventricular fibrillation.
fields.adverse: Ectopic beats, tachycardia, anginal pain, palpitations, and gangrene of extremities at prolonged high doses.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, headache, anxiety, and goosebumps.
fields.notes: Must be diluted prior to IV administration; monitor blood pressure and urine output closely.

fields.action: Direct-acting synthetic inotrope that is a selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor agonist, with minor beta-2 and alpha-1 activity, producing strong myocardial contractility and mild vasodilation.
fields.forms: Solution for IV infusion: 12.5 mg/mL (in 20 mL vials). Premixed IV bags: 1 mg/mL, 2 mg/mL, 4 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Short-term management of adults with cardiac decompensation due to depressed contractility (such as heart failure or post-cardiac surgery).
fields.contraindication: Idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis (IHSS) and known hypersensitivity to dobutamine.
fields.adverse: Marked increases in heart rate or blood pressure, precipitation of ventricular arrhythmias, and myocardial ischemia.
fields.effects: Increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, headache, nausea, and shortness of breath.
fields.notes: Contains sodium bisulfite which can cause allergic-type reactions in susceptible patients; used primarily in short-term hospital infusions.

fields.action: Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. It produces profound chronotropic and inotropic cardiac stimulation alongside systemic vasodilation and bronchodilation.
fields.forms: Injection solution: 0.2 mg/mL (1:5000).
fields.indication: Management of AV nodal block, Stokes-Adams attacks, cardiac arrest (prior to electrical pacing), and bronchospasm during anesthesia.
fields.contraindication: Tachycardia or heart block caused by digitalis toxicity, and ventricular arrhythmias requiring inotropic therapy.
fields.adverse: Serious tachyarrhythmias, angina pectoris, severe hypotension, and cardiac arrest.
fields.effects: Flushing, sweating, tachycardia, palpitations, nervousness, and dizziness.
fields.notes: Largely replaced in modern practice by more selective cardiac and respiratory agents, but retains utility in specific bradyarrhythmia emergencies.

fields.action: Powerful direct-acting alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist that causes marked arterial vasoconstriction, raising systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and induces mydriasis.
fields.forms: Injection: 10 mg/mL. Ophthalmic solution: 2.5%, 10%. Nasal spray: 0.125%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 1%.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypotension during anesthesia, systemic shock states, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, relief of nasal congestion, and production of mydriasis for eye exams.
fields.contraindication: Severe hypertension, ventricular tachycardia, narrow-angle glaucoma, and concurrent use with MAO inhibitors.
fields.adverse: Hypertensive crisis, acute pulmonary edema, severe reflex bradycardia, and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Headache, excitability, restlessness, reflex bradycardia, and stinging upon nasal/eye application.
fields.notes: Often triggers reflex bradycardia due to the body's baroreceptor response to sudden, sharp increases in blood pressure.

fields.action: Selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by stimulating intracellular adenylate cyclase and increasing cyclic AMP.
fields.forms: Metered-dose inhaler (MDI): 90 mcg/actuation. Nebulization solution: 0.083%, 0.5%. Oral tablets: 2 mg, 4 mg. Syrup: 2 mg/5 mL.
fields.indication: Treatment and prevention of bronchospasm in reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma, COPD) and prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to albuterol components and severe tachyarrhythmias.
fields.adverse: Paradoxical bronchospasm, hypokalemia, cardiac arrhythmias, and severe hypersensitivity reactions.
fields.effects: Tremors, nervousness, tachycardia, palpitations, headache, and throat irritation.
fields.notes: Widely used as a short-acting rescue inhaler for acute asthma symptoms.

fields.action: Relatively selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes smooth muscle of the bronchi, uterus, and vascular bed.
fields.forms: Inhalation aerosol: 0.65 mg/actuation. Syrup: 10 mg/5 mL. Tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.indication: Bronchodilator for bronchial asthma and reversible bronchospasm associated with bronchitis and emphysema.
fields.contraindication: Cardiac arrhythmias associated with tachycardia and known hypersensitivity to sympathomimetic amines.
fields.adverse: Tachycardia, palpitations, hypertension, and paradoxical bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Nervousness, tremor, nausea, vomiting, and bad taste in the mouth.
fields.notes: Possesses slightly less beta-2 selectivity than albuterol, meaning it can have a higher incidence of cardiac side effects.

fields.action: Relatively selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and inhibits uterine contractions.
fields.forms: Injection solution: 1 mg/mL. Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg.
fields.indication: Prevention and relief of bronchospasm in bronchial asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to sympathomimetic amines and use for tocolysis (off-label use restricted due to maternal cardiac risks).
fields.adverse: Pulmonary edema (in obstetric contexts), maternal/fetal tachycardia, and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, nervousness, headache, tachycardia, and muscle cramps.
fields.notes: Black box warnings exist regarding oral use for suppressing preterm labor due to severe cardiac adverse events.

fields.action: Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics lasting 12 to 24 hours.
fields.forms: Salmeterol: Inhalation powder (Diskus) 50 mcg.
fields.contraindication: Primary treatment of acute asthma symptoms without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid (monotherapy in asthma carries increased mortality risk).
fields.adverse: Severe paradoxical bronchospasm, life-threatening asthma exacerbations (if used without ICS), and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, dizziness, headache, tachycardia, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden asthma attacks.

fields.action: Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics lasting 12 to 24 hours.
fields.forms: Formoterol: Inhalation capsule/solution 12 mcg.
fields.contraindication: Primary treatment of acute asthma symptoms without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid (monotherapy in asthma carries increased mortality risk).
fields.adverse: Severe paradoxical bronchospasm, life-threatening asthma exacerbations (if used without ICS), and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, dizziness, headache, tachycardia, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden asthma attacks.

fields.action: Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics lasting 12 to 24 hours.
fields.forms: Indacaterol: Inhalation powder 75 mcg, 150 mcg.
fields.contraindication: Primary treatment of acute asthma symptoms without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid (monotherapy in asthma carries increased mortality risk).
fields.adverse: Severe paradoxical bronchospasm, life-threatening asthma exacerbations (if used without ICS), and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, dizziness, headache, tachycardia, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden asthma attacks.

fields.action: Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics lasting 12 to 24 hours.
fields.forms: Vilanterol: Available in combination inhalers (e.g., with umeclidinium or fluticasone).
fields.contraindication: Primary treatment of acute asthma symptoms without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid (monotherapy in asthma carries increased mortality risk).
fields.adverse: Severe paradoxical bronchospasm, life-threatening asthma exacerbations (if used without ICS), and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, dizziness, headache, tachycardia, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden asthma attacks.

fields.action: Long-acting, selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists. They provide prolonged relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle through high lipid solubility or receptor-binding kinetics lasting 12 to 24 hours.
fields.forms: Olodaterol: Respimat soft mist 2.5 mcg/actuation.
fields.contraindication: Primary treatment of acute asthma symptoms without a concurrent inhaled corticosteroid (monotherapy in asthma carries increased mortality risk).
fields.adverse: Severe paradoxical bronchospasm, life-threatening asthma exacerbations (if used without ICS), and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Tremor, dizziness, headache, tachycardia, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: These are maintenance agents, not rescue medications; salmeterol and formoterol should never be used alone to treat acute, sudden asthma attacks.

fields.action: Indirect-acting sympathomimetic agents that promote the release of stored catecholamines (norepinephrine and dopamine) from nerve terminals into the synaptic cleft, while inhibiting their reuptake.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg. Extended-release capsules: 5 mg to 30 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
fields.contraindication: Advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, moderate-to-severe hypertension, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, and history of drug abuse.
fields.adverse: Psychotic episodes, cardiomyopathy, hypertensive crisis, and severe psychological dependence/abuse potential.
fields.effects: Insomnia, decreased appetite, weight loss, dry mouth, tachycardia, and nervousness.
fields.notes: Classified as Schedule II controlled substances due to high potential for abuse and psychological dependence.

fields.action: Central nervous system stimulant and indirect sympathomimetic that causes marked release of dopamine and other monoamines into synapses, blocking their reuptake.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 5 mg.
fields.indication: Short-term adjunct in the management of exogenous obesity and treatment of ADHD (rarely prescribed).
fields.contraindication: Advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, hypertension, hyperthyroidism, and history of substance abuse.
fields.adverse: Severe cardiovascular toxicity, stroke, paranoia, hallucinations, and severe addiction/dependence.
fields.effects: Insomnia, irritability, hyperactive motor activity, tremor, sweating, and anorexia.
fields.notes: High abuse liability; listed as a Schedule II controlled substance with tightly restricted clinical indications.

fields.action: Mixed-acting sympathomimetic agent. It directly stimulates alpha and beta receptors, and indirectly causes the release of endogenous norepinephrine from storage vesicles.
fields.forms: Injection solution: 50 mg/mL. Oral capsules: 25 mg, 50 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of acute hypotension, particularly during spinal or general anesthesia, and relief of bronchospasm.
fields.contraindication: Angle-closure glaucoma, concurrent use with MAO inhibitors, severe hypertension, and tachyarrhythmias.
fields.adverse: Hypertensive crisis, stroke, tachyarrhythmias, and urinary retention.
fields.effects: Nervousness, insomnia, dizziness, palpitations, and sweating.
fields.notes: Prone to tachyphylaxis (rapidly diminishing physiological response with repeated doses due to depletion of stored norepinephrine).

fields.action: Blocks the presynaptic reuptake pump for catecholamines (norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin), resulting in high concentrations of neurotransmitters in synapses. It also acts as a local anesthetic by blocking sodium channels.
fields.forms: Topical solution: 4%, 10% (restricted clinical use).
fields.indication: Local anesthesia of mucous membranes of the oral, laryngeal, and nasal cavities (historical/specialized clinical use).
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to ester-type local anesthetics, intravenous or subcutaneous administration (high systemic toxicity), and severe cardiovascular disease.
fields.adverse: Severe coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction, stroke, malignant hyperthermia, seizures, and ventricular fibrillation.
fields.effects: Euphoria, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, anxiety, and local tissue ischemia.
fields.notes: Highly addictive controlled substance (Schedule II); clinical use is restricted strictly to topical mucosal anesthesia where its intrinsic vasoconstrictive property is advantageous.

fields.action: Indirect-acting sympathomimetic amine that enters nerve terminals and displaces stored norepinephrine, forcing its massive release into the synapse.
fields.forms: Not an approved therapeutic drug product (found naturally in aged, fermented, or cured foods like cheese, wine, and cured meats).
fields.indication: None clinically (studied primarily for its adverse dietary interactions).
fields.contraindication: Patients taking Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs).
fields.adverse: Severe, life-threatening hypertensive crisis ("cheese effect"), intracranial hemorrhage, and cardiac arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Severe pulsatile headache, palpitations, sweating, nausea, and vomiting.
fields.notes: Normally degraded rapidly by MAO enzymes in the gut wall and liver; patients taking MAOIs cannot break it down, allowing dietary tyramine to trigger a catastrophic spike in blood pressure.

fields.action: Competitive, non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It produces vasodilation by blocking alpha-receptors on vascular smooth muscle, lowering peripheral resistance.
fields.forms: Intravenous/Intramuscular injection: 5 mg/vial (reconstituted). Ophthalmic solution: 0.75% (for mydriasis reversal).
fields.indication: Prevention or control of hypertensive episodes due to pheochromocytoma (such as during preoperative preparation or surgical excision), prevention of dermal necrosis following norepinephrine extravasation, and reversal of soft-tissue local anesthesia.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to phentolamine, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, angina pectoris, or a history of myocardial infarction.
fields.adverse: Severe reflex tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, exacerbation of myocardial ischemia, angina, and cerebrovascular spasm.
fields.effects: Flushing, dizziness, nasal stuffiness, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, and vomiting.
fields.notes: Frequently infiltrated subcutaneously around an area of norepinephrine extravasation within 12 hours to block localized vasoconstriction and prevent tissue necrosis.

fields.action: Non-competitive, irreversible alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It forms a stable covalent bond with alpha-receptors, leading to a long-lasting blockade that cannot be overcome by high concentrations of circulating agonists.
fields.forms: Oral capsules: 10 mg.
fields.indication: Management of pheochromocytoma (to control blood pressure episodes and symptoms of catecholamine excess prior to and during surgery), and chronic urinary retention due to prostatic obstruction (off-label).
fields.contraindication: Conditions where a fall in blood pressure would be dangerous (such as uncompensated heart failure or severe coronary artery disease), and hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Marked postural (orthostatic) hypotension accompanied by dizziness or fainting, reflex tachycardia, and inhibition of ejaculation.
fields.effects: Nasal congestion, miosis, dry mouth, tiredness, and lethargy.
fields.notes: Because it binds irreversibly, its blockade lasts for several days after discontinuation, requiring slow dosage titration and adequate volume repletion prior to surgical procedures.

fields.action: Competitive, selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It blocks postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle and bladder neck tissue, leading to vasodilation of both arterioles and veins.
fields.forms: Oral capsules: 1 mg, 2 mg, 5 mg.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension, and treatment of symptoms related to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and Raynaud's phenomenon.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to quinazolines or prazosin.
fields.adverse: Severe "first-dose syncope" (profound orthostatic hypotension with sudden loss of consciousness shortly after the initial dose), marked dizziness, and palpitations.
fields.effects: Dizziness, headache, drowsiness, weakness, nausea, and nasal congestion.
fields.notes: To minimize the risk of first-dose syncope, the initial dose should be very small (e.g., 1 mg) and taken right before bedtime.

fields.action: Competitive, selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and bladder neck tissue.
fields.forms: Oral capsules: 1 mg, 2 mg, 5 mg.
fields.indication: Essential hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms, and Raynaud's phenomenon.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to quinazolines or prazosin.
fields.adverse: First-dose syncope (severe orthostatic hypotension with sudden loss of consciousness), marked dizziness, and palpitations.
fields.effects: Dizziness, headache, drowsiness, weakness, and nasal congestion.
fields.notes: The first dose should always be taken at bedtime to prevent sudden fainting episodes.

fields.action: Competitive blockade of postsynaptic alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate capsule (improving urine flow) while dilating peripheral blood vessels (lowering blood pressure).
fields.forms: Doxazosin: Tablets: 1 mg, 2 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg; Extended-release tablets: 4 mg, 8 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension and functional symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to quinazolines, doxazosin, or terazosin, and history of orthostatic hypotension.
fields.adverse: First-dose orthostatic hypotension, syncope, priapism (prolonged, painful erection), and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract surgery.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, peripheral edema, headache, nasal congestion, and asthenia.
fields.notes: Like prazosin, the first dose should be administered at bedtime to mitigate severe dizziness or sudden fainting spells.

fields.action: Selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist that produces vasodilation and relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 1 mg, 2 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg. Extended-release tablets: 4 mg, 8 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
fields.contraindication: History of orthostatic hypotension and hypersensitivity to quinazolines.
fields.adverse: Severe orthostatic hypotension, syncope, priapism, and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS).
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, edema, headache, and vertigo.
fields.notes: Like prazosin, initial dosing should start low and be taken at bedtime to mitigate acute postural blood pressure drops.

fields.action: Competitive blockade of postsynaptic alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate capsule (improving urine flow) while dilating peripheral blood vessels (lowering blood pressure).
fields.forms: Terazosin: Capsules: 1 mg, 2 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension and functional symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to quinazolines, doxazosin, or terazosin, and history of orthostatic hypotension.
fields.adverse: First-dose orthostatic hypotension, syncope, priapism (prolonged, painful erection), and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract surgery.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, peripheral edema, headache, nasal congestion, and asthenia.
fields.notes: Like prazosin, the first dose should be administered at bedtime to mitigate severe dizziness or sudden fainting spells.

fields.action: Highly selective antagonists for alpha-1A and alpha-1D receptor subtypes located predominantly in the prostate, prostatic urethra, and bladder base, causing minimal systemic vasodilation compared to non-subtype selective alpha blockers.
fields.forms: Tamsulosin: Capsules (modified release): 0.4 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
fields.adverse: Severe abnormal ejaculation (retrograde ejaculation), orthostatic hypotension (though less frequent than with doxazosin/prazosin), and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS).
fields.effects: Dizziness, headache, nasopharyngitis, rhinitis, and diarrhea.
fields.notes: Because of their high selectivity for prostate tissue, they have minimal impact on blood pressure, making dose adjustments for hypertension unnecessary.

fields.action: Highly selective antagonists for alpha-1A and alpha-1D receptor subtypes located predominantly in the prostate, prostatic urethra, and bladder base, causing minimal systemic vasodilation compared to non-subtype selective alpha blockers.
fields.forms: Silodosin: Capsules: 4 mg, 8 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
fields.contraindication: Severe hepatic impairment (for silodosin), severe renal impairment, and concurrent use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (like ketoconazole).
fields.adverse: Severe abnormal ejaculation (retrograde ejaculation), orthostatic hypotension (though less frequent than with doxazosin/prazosin), and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS).
fields.effects: Dizziness, headache, nasopharyngitis, rhinitis, and diarrhea.
fields.notes: Because of their high selectivity for prostate tissue, they have minimal impact on blood pressure, making dose adjustments for hypertension unnecessary.

fields.action: Competitive, selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. By blocking presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, it increases the release of norepinephrine in the central and peripheral nervous systems, raising blood pressure, heart rate, and sympathetic tone.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 5.4 mg (formulations vary widely as prescription medications or herbal/dietary supplements).
fields.indication: Historically used for the management of erectile dysfunction and orthostatic hypotension.
fields.contraindication: Renal disease, cardiorenal dysfunction, history of ulcer disease, psychiatric disorders, and hypertension.
fields.adverse: Hypertensive crisis, severe anxiety, panic attacks, tachycardia, and motor tremors.
fields.effects: Headaches, dizziness, nervousness, irritability, nausea, and frequent urination.
fields.notes: It is a naturally occurring alkaloid (from the bark of Pausinystalia yohimbe) that can trigger severe central nervous system excitation and pronounced blood pressure spikes.

fields.action: Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist with membrane-stabilizing activity. It blocks the chronotropic, inotropic, and vasodilatory responses to beta-adrenergic stimulation and crosses the blood-brain barrier easily.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg. Extended-release capsules: 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg, 160 mg. Injection: 1 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Hypertension, angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction prophylaxis, migraine headache prophylaxis, essential tremor, and management of hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis symptoms.
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), sinus bradycardia, second-or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, and overt heart failure.
fields.adverse: Severe bronchospasm, heart block, severe bradycardia, precipitation of congestive heart failure, and severe rebound hypertension if abruptly withdrawn.
fields.effects: Fatigue, cold extremities, sleep disturbances, vivid dreams, depression, and sexual dysfunction.
fields.notes: Never stop therapy abruptly; beta-blockers must be tapered over 1 to 2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia or myocardial ischemia.

fields.action: Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist with membrane-stabilizing activity.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg. Extended-release capsules: 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg, 160 mg. Injection: 1 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Hypertension, angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmias, migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, and hyperthyroidism symptoms.
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, severe COPD, sinus bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, and cardiogenic shock.
fields.adverse: Severe bronchospasm, heart block, profound bradycardia, and acute heart failure exacerbation.
fields.effects: Fatigue, cold extremities, vivid dreams, depression, and sleep disturbances.
fields.notes: Must never be discontinued abruptly; tapering over 1 to 2 weeks is mandatory to prevent rebound hypertension or myocardial ischemia.

fields.action: Competitive beta-adrenergic receptor blockers that reduce the production of aqueous humor in the ciliary epithelium of the eye, lowering intraocular pressure. Systemically, they block beta receptors to lower heart rate and contractility.
fields.forms: Timolol: Ophthalmic solution: 0.25%, 0.5%. Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.contraindication: Asthma, history of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sinus bradycardia, and cardiogenic shock.
fields.adverse: Systemic absorption from eye drops causing severe bronchospasm, bradycardia, heart block, and heart failure flare-ups.
fields.effects: Stinging or burning upon eye drop instillation, blurred vision, dry eyes, fatigue, and headache.
fields.notes: When applying eye drops, patients should use nasolacrimal occlusion (gentle tear duct compression) to minimize systemic absorption into the bloodstream.

fields.action: Competitive beta-adrenergic receptor blockers that reduce the production of aqueous humor in the ciliary epithelium of the eye, lowering intraocular pressure. Systemically, they block beta receptors to lower heart rate and contractility.
fields.forms: Betaxolol: Ophthalmic solution: 0.5%. Oral tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.contraindication: Asthma, history of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sinus bradycardia, and cardiogenic shock.
fields.adverse: Systemic absorption from eye drops causing severe bronchospasm, bradycardia, heart block, and heart failure flare-ups.
fields.effects: Stinging or burning upon eye drop instillation, blurred vision, dry eyes, fatigue, and headache.
fields.notes: When applying eye drops, patients should use nasolacrimal occlusion (gentle tear duct compression) to minimize systemic absorption into the bloodstream.

fields.action: Non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist with significant Intrinsic Sympathomimetic Activity (ISA) (partial agonist activity), meaning it blocks strong catecholamines while providing mild baseline stimulation of beta receptors itself.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, cardiogenic shock, second- and third-degree heart block, and severe bradycardia.
fields.adverse: Severe bronchospasm, heart block, and acute worsening of heart failure in susceptible patients.
fields.effects: Dizziness, weakness, insomnia, vivid dreams, muscle pain, and lower incidence of resting bradycardia compared to other beta blockers.
fields.notes: Due to its intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA), it causes less resting bradycardia and cold-extremity side effects than pure antagonists like propranolol.

fields.action: Long-acting, non-selective beta-adrenergic receptor blocker without membrane-stabilizing activity or significant intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg, 160 mg.
fields.indication: Management of hypertension and long-term prophylactic treatment of angina pectoris.
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia, and greater than first-degree heart block.
fields.adverse: Severe bradycardia, heart block, precipitating heart failure, and acute bronchoconstriction.
fields.effects: Fatigue, dizziness, bradycardia, cold extremities, and emotional depression.
fields.notes: Excreted primarily unchanged by the kidneys, meaning dosing intervals must be extended significantly in patients with renal impairment.

fields.action: Cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that preferentially blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure, with less effect on bronchial and vascular beta-2 receptors at lower doses.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg. Intravenous injection: 0.5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of hypertension, long-term management of angina pectoris, and secondary prevention of myocardial infarction.
fields.contraindication: Sinus bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, and overt cardiac failure.
fields.adverse: Symptomatic bradycardia, severe heart block, heart failure exacerbation, and bronchospasm (at high doses due to loss of selectivity).
fields.effects: Cold hands and feet, fatigue, dizziness, lethargy, and diarrhea.
fields.notes: Hydrophilic agent eliminated primarily by the kidneys; requires dosage reduction in patients with renal function impairment.

fields.action: Cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that reduces heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg. Intravenous injection: 0.5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension, angina pectoris, and acute myocardial infarction.
fields.contraindication: Sinus bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, and overt heart failure.
fields.adverse: Symptomatic bradycardia, severe heart block, heart failure flare-up, and bronchospasm (at high doses).
fields.effects: Cold hands and feet, fatigue, dizziness, and lethargy.
fields.notes: Hydrophilic agent eliminated primarily via the kidneys, requiring dosage adjustments in renal impairment.

fields.action: Ultra-short-acting, cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It inhibits beta-1 receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate and myocardial contractility.
fields.forms: Intravenous injection / infusion: 10 mg/mL, 250 mg/mL. Premixed infusion bags: 10 mg/mL, 20 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Rapid, short-term control of ventricular rate in patients with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, and treatment of perioperative hypertension and tachycardia.
fields.contraindication: Sinus bradycardia, severe cardiogenic shock, uncompensated heart failure, and pre-existing pulmonary hypertension.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, profound bradycardia, cardiac arrest, and local infusion-site inflammation or necrosis.
fields.effects: Asymptomatic or symptomatic hypotension, diaphoresis, dizziness, and nausea.
fields.notes: Features an extremely short elimination half-life of approximately 9 minutes, allowing rapid titration and quick reversal of effects if adverse reactions occur.

fields.action: Selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that reduces heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure.
fields.forms: • Metoprolol tartrate: Tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg. Injection: 1 mg/mL. • Metoprolol succinate (ER): Extended-release tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg.
fields.indication: Hypertension, angina pectoris, heart failure (succinate form), and early intervention in acute myocardial infarction.
fields.contraindication: Severe bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure.
fields.adverse: Severe bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, and exacerbation of asthma or heart failure.
fields.effects: Fatigue, dizziness, depression, diarrhea, shortness of breath, and bradycardia.
fields.notes: Metoprolol tartrate is typically taken twice daily with meals, while the succinate formulation is designed for convenient once-daily dosing.

fields.action: Highly cardioselective beta-1 receptor blocker that also promotes endothelial nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation, reducing peripheral vascular resistance without typical beta-blocker-induced cold extremities.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of essential hypertension, alone or in combination with other agents, to lower blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk.
fields.contraindication: Severe bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, and severe hepatic impairment.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, acute heart failure worsening, and AV block.
fields.effects: Headache, fatigue, dizziness, diarrhea, nausea, and insomnia.
fields.notes: Its unique nitric oxide-releasing property sets it apart from traditional beta-1 blockers by avoiding adverse metabolic profiles and peripheral vasoconstriction.

fields.action: Selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist. It blocks beta-2 receptors, causing inhibition of beta-2-mediated vasodilation, bronchodilation, and glycogenolysis.
fields.forms: Research chemical / specialized pharmacological tool (not an approved commercial therapeutic pharmaceutical drug).
fields.indication: None clinically approved (used primarily as an experimental pharmacological tool to study beta-2 adrenergic pathways).
fields.contraindication: N/A (Not used in human clinical therapeutics).
fields.adverse: Pronounced bronchoconstriction and metabolic disturbances if administered systemically.
fields.effects: Increased airway resistance and muscle cramping.
fields.notes: Primarily of academic and pharmacological value to isolate beta-2 responses in laboratory settings; not utilized in clinical patient care.

fields.action: Competitive antagonist at alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors. It produces peripheral vasodilation (via alpha-1 block) while preventing reflex tachycardia through simultaneous beta-blockade.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 100 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg. Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension, hypertensive emergencies, and blood pressure control during pregnancy-induced hypertension (preeclampsia).
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, overt cardiac failure, greater than first-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, and severe bradycardia.
fields.adverse: Severe orthostatic hypotension, acute bronchospasm, heart block, and hepatocellular injury (liver damage).
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, nausea, scalp tingling, nasal stuffiness, and vivid dreams.
fields.notes: Widely utilized in obstetrics for hypertensive crises during pregnancy because it reduces blood pressure effectively without heavily compromising uteroplacental blood flow.

fields.action: Competitive antagonist at alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, providing peripheral vasodilation and beta-blockade.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 100 mg, 200 mg, 300 mg. Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Essential hypertension, hypertensive emergencies, and pregnancy-induced hypertension (preeclampsia).
fields.contraindication: Bronchial asthma, overt cardiac failure, greater than first-degree heart block, and cardiogenic shock.
fields.adverse: Severe orthostatic hypotension, bronchospasm, heart block, and hepatocellular injury (liver damage).
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, nausea, scalp tingling, and nasal stuffiness.
fields.notes: Frequently used in obstetrics because it lowers blood pressure safely without significantly compromising uteroplacental blood flow.

fields.action: Non-selective beta blocker and alpha-1 blocker with antioxidant properties. It blocks beta-1, beta-2, and alpha-1 receptors, causing vasodilation and reducing cardiac workload.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 3.125 mg, 6.25 mg, 12.5 mg, 25 mg. Extended-release capsules: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg.
fields.indication: Management of mild to severe chronic heart failure, left ventricular dysfunction following myocardial infarction, and essential hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Decompensated heart failure requiring intravenous inotropes, bronchial asthma, second-or third-degree AV block, and severe hepatic impairment.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, worsening heart failure symptoms during initiation, bradycardia, and bronchospasm.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, weight gain, diarrhea, hyperlipidemia, and hyperglycemia.
fields.notes: Must be taken with food to slow absorption rate and minimize the risk of sudden orthostatic hypotension or dizziness.

fields.action: Thiazide diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephron, increasing the excretion of sodium, water, chloride, and potassium.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg. Oral solution: 50 mg/5 mL.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension and edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid/estrogen therapy.
fields.contraindication: Anuria, hypersensitivity to sulfonamide-derived drugs, and severe renal or hepatic impairment.
fields.adverse: Severe hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and severe hypersensitivity skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
fields.effects: Frequent urination, dizziness, lightheadedness, mild orthostatic hypotension, headache, and fatigue.
fields.notes: Sulfa-allergic patients may cross-react with thiazides; can elevate blood glucose and uric acid levels.

fields.action: Thiazide-like diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the cortical diluting segment of the ascending loop of Henle and distal tubule, reducing extracellular fluid volume.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension (as step-one therapy or add-on) and management of edema associated with heart failure or renal dysfunction.
fields.contraindication: Anuria, hypersensitivity to sulfonamides or chlorthalidone, and severe electrolyte depletions.
fields.adverse: Hypokalemia, severe hypochloremic alkalosis, hypercalcemia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and exacerbation of gout.
fields.effects: Dizziness, vertigo, paresthesias, headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and increased urination frequency.
fields.notes: Possesses a significantly longer duration of action (up to 72 hours) compared to standard hydrochlorothiazide.

fields.action: Loop diuretic that inhibits the co-transport system (Na^+/K^+/2Cl^-) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, promoting massive excretion of water, sodium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg. Oral solution: 8 mg/mL, 10 mg/mL. Injection solution: 10 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Treatment of acute pulmonary edema, edema associated with heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, renal disease, and severe hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Anuria, hepatic coma, severe electrolyte depletion, and known hypersensitivity to furosemide or sulfonamides.
fields.adverse: Profound volume depletion, circulatory collapse, severe hypokalemia, ototoxicity (tinnitus/hearing loss), and thrombotic events.
fields.effects: Increased urination frequency, dizziness, lightheadedness, nausea, dyspepsia, and blurred vision.
fields.notes: Rapid IV administration can trigger transient or permanent ototoxicity; patients should be monitored closely for signs of severe dehydration.

fields.action: Potassium-sparing diuretic and competitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that blocks aldosterone binding in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts, increasing sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg.
fields.indication: Management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, and edema due to cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome.
fields.contraindication: Acute renal insufficiency, anuria, hyperkalemia, and concurrent use of eplerenone.
fields.adverse: Severe hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, agranulocytosis, and acute renal dysfunction.
fields.effects: Gynecomastia, breast pain/tenderness, menstrual irregularities, dizziness, lethargy, and mild gastrointestinal cramps.
fields.notes: Unique for being a potassium-sparing diuretic that can cause endocrine side effects (such as gynecomastia in men) due to its secondary anti-androgen activity.

fields.action: Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. It stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem vasomotor center, reducing sympathetic outflow from the central nervous system, which lowers peripheral resistance, heart rate, and blood pressure.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 0.1 mg, 0.2 mg, 0.3 mg. Transdermal patches (weekly): 0.1 mg/24hr, 0.2 mg/24hr, 0.3 mg/24hr. Injection solution: 100 mcg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD - off-label/specific formulations), and management of severe cancer pain or opioid withdrawal symptoms.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to clonidine and severe sinus bradycardia or AV block (unless a functioning pacemaker is present).
fields.adverse: Severe rebound hypertension upon abrupt discontinuation, profound bradycardia, and depressive symptoms.
fields.effects: Dry mouth, drowsiness, sedation, dizziness, constipation, fatigue, and sexual dysfunction.
fields.notes: Must never be stopped abruptly; sudden withdrawal can trigger a dangerous hypertensive crisis characterized by extreme surges in catecholamines.

fields.action: Central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. It is metabolized intracellularly to alphamethylnorepinephrine, which replaces norepinephrine in vesicles and stimulates central inhibitory alpha-2 receptors, reducing sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg. Intravenous injection: 50 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of hypertension, including hypertension during pregnancy (preeclampsia/gestational hypertension).
fields.contraindication: Active hepatic disease (such as acute hepatitis or active cirrhosis), previous methyldopa-induced liver disorders, and concurrent use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs).
fields.adverse: Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia (positive direct Coombs test), severe hepatitis, liver necrosis, and parkinsonian signs.
fields.effects: Drowsiness, sedation, dry mouth, nasal stuffiness, edema, dizziness, and postpartum depression.
fields.notes: Widely preferred historically and currently for treating hypertension during pregnancy due to its well-established fetal safety profile, despite routine monitoring required for liver enzymes and Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia.

fields.action: Inhibits the transport of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin into storage vesicles (VMAT2) within postganglionic sympathetic nerve endings, leading to depletion of peripheral and central monoamine stores.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 0.1 mg, 0.25 mg.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension (historically common, now specialized).
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity, history of mental depression (especially with suicidal tendencies), active peptic ulcer disease, ulcerative colitis, and concurrent use with MAO inhibitors.
fields.adverse: Severe depressive states, psychic depression, Parkinson-like extrapyramidal symptoms, peptic ulcer activation, and severe bradycardia.
fields.effects: Nasal congestion, drowsiness, dizziness, lethargy, diarrhea, impotence, and weight gain.
fields.notes: Can cross the blood-brain barrier easily, which accounts for its significant central nervous system side effects, including severe mental depression.

fields.action: Adrenergic neuron blocker that accumulates in sympathetic nerve terminals and replaces norepinephrine in storage vesicles, blocking the release of norepinephrine in response to nerve stimulation.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 10 mg, 25 mg.
fields.indication: Management of moderate to severe essential hypertension (typically for patients unresponsive to other agents).
fields.contraindication: Established or suspected pheochromocytoma, congestive heart failure, concurrent use with MAO inhibitors, and severe coronary artery disease.
fields.adverse: Marked orthostatic hypotension, severe syncope, and exacerbation of heart failure.
fields.effects: Exertional dizziness, daytime fatigue, diarrhea, fluid retention, peripheral edema, and sexual dysfunction.
fields.notes: Prone to causing pronounced orthostatic hypotension, especially upon standing up or exercising.

fields.action: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium ions into vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle, leading to coronary and peripheral vasodilation.
fields.forms: Extended-release/sustained-release tablets: 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg. Capsules (immediate-release): 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.indication: Management of hypertension, vasospastic angina, and chronic stable angina.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to dihydropyridines, cardiogenic shock, and use of immediate-release formulations for acute hypertension management.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, reflex tachycardia, myocardial ischemia (with rapid-acting forms), and peripheral edema.
fields.effects: Flushing, headache, dizziness, peripheral ankle edema, and fatigue.
fields.notes: Immediate-release capsules are no longer recommended for routine hypertension control due to risks associated with sudden, sharp blood pressure drops and reflex tachycardia.

fields.action: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits transmembrane calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, leading to profound relaxation of coronary and peripheral resistance arteries.
fields.forms: Extended-release tablets: 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg. Immediate-release capsules: 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina, chronic stable angina, and essential hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Cardiogenic shock, hypersensitivity to dihydropyridines, and acute myocardial infarction.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, reflex tachycardia, myocardial ischemia, and peripheral edema.
fields.effects: Flushing, headache, dizziness, lower extremity edema, and fatigue.
fields.notes: Immediate-release forms should be avoided for treating acute blood pressure spikes due to risks associated with rapid, uncontrolled drops in pressure and reflex tachycardia.

fields.action: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits calcium ion influx into myocardial and vascular smooth muscle cells, slowing AV nodal conduction and dilating coronary/peripheral vessels.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg. Sustained-release tablets: 120 mg, 180 mg, 240 mg. Intravenous injection: 2.5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Treatment of essential hypertension, angina pectoris, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (such as atrial fibrillation rate control).
fields.contraindication: Severe hypotension, cardiogenic shock, second- or third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, and ventricular tachycardia.
fields.adverse: Severe heart block, profound bradycardia, acute heart failure exacerbation, and cardiovascular collapse.
fields.effects: Constipation (very common), dizziness, nausea, headache, and peripheral edema.
fields.notes: Prominent negative inotropic and dromotropic effects; should not be combined with beta-blockers without close clinical monitoring due to the risk of severe heart block or bradycardia.

fields.action: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits calcium ion influx through slow channels into myocardial and vascular smooth muscle cells, reducing myocardial oxygen demand, slowing AV nodal conduction, and dilating coronary arteries.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg. Sustained-release tablets: 120 mg, 180 mg, 240 mg. Intravenous injection: 2.5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Treatment of angina pectoris, essential hypertension, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
fields.contraindication: Severe hypotension, cardiogenic shock, second- or third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, and ventricular tachycardia.
fields.adverse: Severe heart block, profound bradycardia, acute heart failure exacerbation, and cardiovascular collapse.
fields.effects: Constipation (very common), dizziness, nausea, headache, and peripheral edema.
fields.notes: Possesses prominent negative inotropic and dromotropic properties; should not be combined with beta-blockers without close clinical oversight due to the risk of severe heart block.

fields.action: Direct-acting arterial vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle primarily in arterioles, decreasing systemic vascular resistance.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg. Intravenous/Intramuscular injection: 20 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of moderate to severe essential hypertension, hypertensive emergencies, and heart failure (often combined with isosorbide dinitrate).
fields.contraindication: Coronary artery disease, mitral valvular rheumatic heart disease, and idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
fields.adverse: Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome (arthritis, fever, rash), reflex tachycardia, angina precipitation, and severe hypotension.
fields.effects: Headache, palpitations, flushing, anorexia, nausea, and tachycardia.
fields.notes: Frequently triggers reflex tachycardia and fluid retention; usually administered alongside a beta-blocker and a diuretic to offset these compensatory responses.

fields.action: Potent direct-acting peripheral vasodilator that opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing hyperpolarization and relaxation of arterial smooth muscle.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 10 mg. Topical solution/foam: 2%, 5% (for hair growth).
fields.indication: Severe, drug-resistant hypertension (oral), and treatment of androgenetic alopecia (topical).
fields.contraindication: Pheochromocytoma (can stimulate catecholamine release), acute myocardial infarction, and hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Marked reflex tachycardia, severe fluid retention, congestive heart failure exacerbation, pericardial effusion, and cardiac tamponade.
fields.effects: Hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth on face/body), headache, edema, tachycardia, and weight gain.
fields.notes: Because it causes profound reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, oral minoxidil must always be co-administered with a loop diuretic and a beta-blocker.

fields.action: Potent, fast-acting parenteral vasodilator that breaks down to release nitric oxide (NO), activating intracellular guanylyl cyclase, increasing cyclic GMP, and relaxing both arterial and venous smooth muscle.
fields.forms: Lyophilized powder for injection: 50 mg per vial.
fields.indication: Management of hypertensive emergencies, production of controlled hypotension during anesthesia to reduce bleeding, and acute congestive heart failure.
fields.contraindication: Compensatory hypertension (such as arteriovenous shunt or coarctation of the aorta), congenital optic atrophy, and tobacco amblyopia.
fields.adverse: Severe cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity, profound acute hypotension, and methemoglobinemia.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, abdominal pain, and apprehension.
fields.notes: Light-sensitive solution; infusion bags must be wrapped in opaque foil during administration. Prolonged infusions risk cyanide accumulation.

fields.action: Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, causing hyperpolarization and relaxation of arteriolar smooth muscle (direct vasodilator). It also inhibits insulin release from the pancreatic beta cells.
fields.forms: Oral capsules: 50 mg. Oral suspension: 50 mg/mL. Intravenous injection: 15 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of severe, acute hypertensive emergencies (IV form) and treatment of chronic hypoglycemia caused by hyperinsulinism (oral form).
fields.contraindication: Functional hypoglycemia, hypersensitivity to diazoxide or thiazides, and conditions where maintenance of blood pressure or increased cardiac output is compromised.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, sodium and fluid retention, ketoacidosis, and hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma.
fields.effects: Hyperglycemia, tachycardia, flushing, dizziness, hirsutism (excessive hair growth with chronic oral use), and gastrointestinal upset.
fields.notes: Because of its potent inhibitory effect on insulin secretion, it is uniquely utilized for intractable hypoglycemia, while its powerful vasodilatory properties make it useful for acute hypertensive crises.

fields.forms: Intravenous injection /infusion concentrate: 10 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Short-term management of severe hypertension (hypertensive emergencies) when rapid parenteral reduction of blood pressure is clinically necessary, including use during perioperative care.
fields.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to fenoldopam or its components.
fields.adverse: Symptomatic hypotension, tachycardia, intraocular pressure elevation (in glaucoma patients), and hypokalemia.
fields.effects: Headache, flushing, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and anxiety.
fields.notes: Uniquely increases renal blood flow and sodium excretion while lowering blood pressure, making it particularly useful in patients with renal impairment during hypertensive emergencies.

fields.action: Direct renin inhibitor that binds tightly to the active site of renin, blocking the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I at the rate-limiting step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 150 mg, 300 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of essential hypertension, alone or combined with other antihypertensive agents.
fields.contraindication: Pregnancy (due to fetal toxicity), and concurrent use with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in patients with diabetes mellitus or moderate-to-severe renal impairment.
fields.adverse: Angioedema, severe hyperkalemia, severe hypotension, and acute renal impairment.
fields.effects: Diarrhea (most common at higher doses), cough, dizziness, fatigue, and nasopharyngitis.
fields.notes: Carries a black box warning regarding fetal toxicity; must be discontinued immediately if pregnancy is detected.

fields.action: Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), preventing the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which decreases vasoconstriction and reduces aldosterone secretion while increasing bradykinin levels.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension, congestive heart failure, left ventricular dysfunction post-myocardial infarction, and diabetic nephropathy.
fields.contraindication: History of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema, hereditary or idiopathic angioedema, concurrent use with aliskiren in patients with diabetes, and pregnancy.
fields.adverse: Life-threatening angioedema (swelling of face, lips, tongue), severe hyperkalemia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis, and acute renal failure.
fields.effects: Persistent dry hacking cough, dizziness, headache, fatigue, and altered taste (dysgeusia).
fields.notes: Contains a sulfhydryl group associated with specific adverse reactions like rash and dysgeusia; should be taken 1 hour before a meal.

fields.action: Inhibits ACE, blocking the formation of angiotensin II, lowering systemic vascular resistance, and reducing blood pressure.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg. Intravenous injection (as enalaprilat): 1.25 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension, symptomatic congestive heart failure, and asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.
fields.contraindication: History of angioedema related to previous ACE inhibitor therapy, pregnancy, and hypersensitivity.
fields.adverse: Angioedema, hyperkalemia, severe hypotension (especially with first-dose diuresis), and renal failure.
fields.effects: Persistent dry cough, dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, and asthenia.
fields.notes: Long-acting ACE inhibitor that allows for convenient once- or twice-daily dosing compared to captopril.

fields.forms: Oral tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of hypertension, reduction of stroke risk in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy, and treatment of diabetic nephropathy.
fields.contraindication: Pregnancy (fetal toxicity) and concurrent use with aliskiren in patients with diabetes.
fields.adverse: Hyperkalemia, severe angioedema, acute kidney injury, and profound hypotension.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, nasal congestion, back pain, and upper respiratory infections.
fields.notes: Does not inhibit ACE or cause the persistent dry cough characteristic of ACE inhibitors, making it an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors.

fields.forms: Candesartan: Tablets: 4 mg, 8 mg, 16 mg, 32 mg.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension and heart failure.
fields.contraindication: Pregnancy (black box warning for fetal injury/death) and concurrent use with aliskiren in diabetes.
fields.adverse: Severe hyperkalemia, acute renal failure, symptomatic hypotension, and angioedema.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, upper respiratory tract infections, diarrhea, and dyspepsia.
fields.notes: Like all ARBs, they provide targeted RAAS blockade without triggering the chronic dry cough seen with ACE inhibitors.

fields.forms: Irbesartan: Tablets: 75 mg, 150 mg, 300 mg.
fields.indication: Management of essential hypertension and nephropathy in type 2 diabetic patients with hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Pregnancy (black box warning for fetal injury/death) and concurrent use with aliskiren in diabetes.
fields.adverse: Severe hyperkalemia, acute renal failure, symptomatic hypotension, and angioedema.
fields.effects: Dizziness, fatigue, upper respiratory tract infections, diarrhea, and dyspepsia.
fields.notes: Like all ARBs, they provide targeted RAAS blockade without triggering the chronic dry cough seen with ACE inhibitors.

fields.action: Converts to nitric oxide (NO) inside vascular smooth muscle, stimulating guanylyl cyclase and increasing cyclic GMP. This leads to relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, predominantly dilating large veins and decreasing preload.
fields.forms: • Sublingual tablets: 0.3 mg, 0.4 mg, 0.6 mg. • Sublingual spray: 0.4 mg/spray. • Transdermal patch: 0.1 mg/hr to 0.8 mg/hr. • Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Acute relief and prophylaxis of angina pectoris, management of acute heart failure, and control of perioperative hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure, hypersensitivity to nitrates, and concurrent use of phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil).
fields.adverse: Severe hypotension, paradoxical bradycardia, reflex tachycardia, and methhemoglobinemia (with high doses).
fields.effects: Throbbing headache, flushing, dizziness, lightheadedness, and postural hypotension.
fields.notes: Patients must maintain a daily "nitrate-free interval" (usually 10 to 12 hours) to prevent the development of pharmacological tolerance.

fields.action: Organic nitrates that release nitric oxide, increasing cyclic GMP levels and causing relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, reducing venous return (preload) and myocardial oxygen demand.
fields.forms: ISMN: Tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg; Extended-release tablets: 30 mg, 60 mg, 120 mg.
fields.indication: Long-term prophylaxis and management of angina pectoris.
fields.contraindication: Concomitant use with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil), severe hypotension, and acute circulatory failure.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotensive episodes, syncopal attacks, and worsening anginal attacks due to reflex responses.
fields.effects: Severe throbbing headaches, dizziness, flushing, lightheadedness upon standing, and nausea.
fields.notes: Like nitroglycerin, these agents require a daily nitrate-free interval to avoid drug tolerance and loss of efficacy.

fields.action: Organic nitrates that release nitric oxide, increasing cyclic GMP levels and causing relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, reducing venous return (preload) and myocardial oxygen demand.
fields.forms: ISDN: Sublingual tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg; Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg.
fields.indication: Long-term prophylaxis and management of angina pectoris; ISDN is also used adjunctively in chronic heart failure.
fields.contraindication: Concomitant use with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil), severe hypotension, and acute circulatory failure.
fields.adverse: Severe hypotensive episodes, syncopal attacks, and worsening anginal attacks due to reflex responses.
fields.effects: Severe throbbing headaches, dizziness, flushing, lightheadedness upon standing, and nausea.
fields.notes: Like nitroglycerin, these agents require a daily nitrate-free interval to avoid drug tolerance and loss of efficacy.

fields.action: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits calcium influx across cardiac and vascular smooth muscle membranes, producing coronary and peripheral vasodilation and slowing heart rate/AV conduction.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg, 120 mg. Extended-release capsules: 120 mg, 180 mg, 240 mg, 300 mg, 360 mg. Intravenous injection: 5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of Prinzmetal's variant angina, chronic stable angina, essential hypertension, and rapid rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter.
fields.contraindication: Sick sinus syndrome, second- or third-degree AV block (without a pacemaker), severe hypotension, acute myocardial infarction, and pulmonary congestion.
fields.adverse: Complete AV heart block, severe bradycardia, acute hypotension, and heart failure exacerbation.
fields.effects: Peripheral edema, headache, dizziness, flushing, asthenia, and mild constipation.
fields.notes: Balances vascular dilation with negative chronotropic and inotropic effects on the heart, making it effective for both angina and rate control.

fields.action: Long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium ions into vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle, causing peripheral arterial vasodilation.
fields.forms: Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg.
fields.indication: Management of hypertension, chronic stable angina, and vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina.
fields.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to amlodipine or other dihydropyridines.
fields.adverse: Marked hypotension, worsening angina upon initiation in patients with severe obstructive coronary artery disease.
fields.effects: Peripheral edema (notably ankle swelling), flushing, fatigue, palpitations, and dizziness.
fields.notes: Features a slow onset and long elimination half-life (around 30 to 50 hours), allowing smooth once-daily dosing without sharp peak-to-trough blood pressure variations.

fields.action: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that selectively inhibits calcium ion influx into vascular smooth muscle, resulting in preferential vasodilation of cerebral and coronary blood vessels over cardiac tissue.
fields.forms: Oral capsules: 20 mg, 30 mg. Extended-release capsules: 45 mg, 60 mg. Intravenous injection/infusion: 2.5 mg/mL.
fields.indication: Management of chronic stable angina and essential hypertension; IV form used for short-term treatment of hypertensive emergencies.
fields.contraindication: Advanced aortic stenosis (due to fixed-output obstruction) and hypersensitivity to nicardipine.
fields.adverse: Severe systemic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, increased angina frequency, and superficial thrombophlebitis at IV sites.
fields.effects: Peripheral edema, headache, flushing, dizziness, and nausea.
fields.notes: Provides significant vascular selectivity, making it highly valuable in neurosurgical or critical care settings for controlling blood pressure.

fields.forms: Extended-release tablets: 500 mg, 1000 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of chronic stable angina pectoris (often used in combination with beta-blockers, nitrates, or calcium channel blockers).
fields.contraindication: Pre-existing hepatic impairment, and concurrent use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) or inducers (e.g., rifampin).
fields.adverse: QT interval prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, and acute renal failure in susceptible patients.
fields.effects: Dizziness, headache, nausea, constipation, and asthenia.
fields.notes: Does not significantly alter resting heart rate or blood pressure, making it a unique metabolic antianginal agent for patients with baseline low heart rates or blood pressure.

fields.forms: Oral tablets: 5 mg, 7.5 mg.
fields.indication: Reduction of hospital admission risk for chronic heart failure in stable patients with reduced ejection fraction, and symptomatic treatment of chronic stable angina.
fields.contraindication: Resting heart rate under 70 beats/min prior to treatment, cardiogenic shock, acute myocardial infarction, severe hypotension, third-degree AV block, and severe hepatic impairment.
fields.adverse: Severe bradycardia, luminous phenomena (phosphenes -temporary visual brightness changes), and atrial fibrillation.
fields.effects: Phosphenes (visual flashes), bradycardia, hypertension, and headache.
fields.notes: Relies strictly on reducing heart rate to lower myocardial oxygen demand; patients should be monitored for visual brightness phenomena.

fields.action: Selective inhibition of phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5), preventing the degradation of cyclic GMP (cGMP) in the corpus cavernosum. This sustains smooth muscle relaxation and allows increased blood flow to erectile tissue in the presence of sexual stimulation.
fields.forms: Sildenafil: Tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of erectile dysfunction and management of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
fields.contraindication: Concurrent use with any form of organic nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators (due to the risk of catastrophic, life-threatening systemic hypotension).
fields.adverse: Severe, profound hypotension, sudden vision loss (non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy - NAION), sudden hearing loss, and prolonged priapism.
fields.effects: Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, visual disturbances (such as blue-tinted vision with sildenafil), and back pain (common with tadalafil).

fields.forms: Tadalafil: Tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.
fields.indication: Treatment of erectile dysfunction and management of pulmonary arterial hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms.
fields.contraindication: Concurrent use with any form of organic nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators (due to the risk of catastrophic, life-threatening systemic hypotension).

fields.indication: Treatment of erectile dysfunction.
fields.contraindication: Concurrent use with any form of organic nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators (due to the risk of catastrophic, life-threatening systemic hypotension).

fields.indication: Rapid conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) to normal sinus rhythm (including tachycardia associated with accessory bypass tracts like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), and diagnostic use during myocardial nuclear imaging.
fields.contraindication: Second- or third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome (unless a functioning artificial pacemaker is present), bronchoconstrictive lung disease (such as asthma), and known hypersensitivity to adenosine.
fields.adverse: Transient asystole, severe bronchospasm, heart block, and ventricular arrhythmias.
fields.effects: Flushing (very common), chest pain, shortness of breath, dyspnea, nausea, headache, and lightheadedness.
fields.notes: Possesses an extremely short elimination half-life of less than 10 seconds; must be administered via a rapid intravenous bolus (typically into a peripheral site close to the heart) followed immediately by a saline flush.

fields.action: Restores and maintains normal intracellular potassium concentration, stabilizing the resting membrane potential of cardiac and skeletal muscle cells and regulating neuromuscular excitability.
fields.indication: Prevention and treatment of hypokalemia (potassium deficiency) due to diuretic use, digitalis toxicity, or excessive losses, and maintenance of cardiac electrophysiological stability.
fields.contraindication: Severe renal impairment (oliguria/anuria), hyperkalemia, acute dehydration, heat cramps, and untreated Addison's disease.
fields.adverse: Hyperkalemia leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation, and cardiac arrest.
fields.effects: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and flatulence (especially with oral formulations).
fields.notes: Intravenous potassium must always be heavily diluted and administered via a controlled infusion pump; never give undiluted IV push potassium, as it can cause rapid cardiac arrest.

fields.action: Acts as an essential cofactor for numerous enzymatic reactions and blocks neuromuscular transmission by decreasing acetylcholine release. It regulates sodium, potassium, and calcium movement across cell membranes and controls cardiac excitability.
fields.forms: Intravenous/Intramuscular injection: 50 mg/mL (5%), 125 mg/mL (12.5%), 250 mg/mL (25%), 500 mg/mL (50%). Oral tablets/capsules vary by supplement.
fields.indication: Treatment and prevention of hypomagnesemia, management of acute torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia), control of seizures in eclampsia/preeclampsia, and adjunctive treatment of severe acute asthma exacerbations.
fields.contraindication: Myocardial damage, heart block, severe renal insufficiency (risk of hypermagnesemia toxicity), and hypermagnesemia.
fields.adverse: Severe respiratory depression, profound hypotension, complete loss of deep tendon reflexes, and circulatory collapse.
fields.effects: Flushing, sweating, transient hypotension, drowsiness, and local injection-site irritation.
fields.notes: Calcium gluconate must always be kept immediately available as a specific antidote to reverse severe magnesium-induced respiratory depression or toxicity.
